title: 7 Signs Someone Secretly Looks Down On You (Even Those You'd Never Suspect)
fullText: Have you ever walked away from a conversation feeling smaller, like nothing actually happened? Nobody yelled at you, nobody said anything mean, but somehow you feel worse about yourself than you did before you started talking to them. [music] And then you try to explain that to someone else. And you can't because what are you going to say? They were too nice to me. They smiled too much. So, you let it go. And you start wondering if maybe you're just being oversensitive. Here's what I want to tell you today. You're not. [music] What you were picking up on has a name. It's called contempt. And it is one of the most psychologically damaging things one person can do to another. Precisely because it almost never looks like anything at all. Not like anger, not like cruelty. It looks like a half smile, a slight pause before they answer you. The way they look just past your shoulder instead of at your eyes. It's subtle. It's quiet. And it is absolutely intentional. Now, most people when they hear the word contempt, they think of something dramatic like someone rolling their eyes or talking down to you in front of a crowd. And yeah, that's contempt, too. But that's the loud version. [music] That's the version you can point to and say, "See that? That right there?" What we're talking about today is the quiet version, the kind that makes you feel crazy for even noticing it. And by the end of this video, you will be able to name exactly what's been happening. and more importantly, you'll know what to do about it. So, let's get into it. Before we go through the signs, I need to make sure we're talking about the same thing because contempt gets confused with a few other emotions that are actually very different. Contempt is not anger. When someone is angry at you, they're still invested. Anger means you matter enough to get a reaction. It means they want something from you, an apology, a change, an acknowledgement. [music] Contempt is different. Contempt is the belief that you are beneath them. Not that you did something wrong, not that they're frustrated with you, but that who you are, your ideas, your feelings, your presence, just [music] doesn't register as important. Think about it this way. Anger says you [music] matter and you let me down. Contempt says you don't matter enough to let down. And that is why it hurts in a way that's so hard to explain [music] because it's not an attack, it's a dismissal. and dismissals are almost impossible to defend yourself against. There's a researcher named John Gottman who spent about 40 years studying how people interact with each other. [music] He watched thousands of couples in a lab just talking, sometimes arguing, sometimes being totally normal. And he became so good at reading the dynamics that he could predict which relationships would fall apart with startling accuracy. And the single biggest thing he looked for, contempt. Not how often people fought, not how loud things got. He looked for those little moments where one person communicated to the other without saying a single word. I am above you. And here's the thing that really got to me when I first learned about this. He found that couples who showed contempt toward each other didn't just have worse relationships. [music] They were physically less healthy. More colds, more infections, more sick days. Because when you're around someone who makes you feel like you don't matter, your body knows. Your stress response activates. [music] And over time, that takes a real measurable toll. So, this isn't just about feelings. This is about your actual well-being. And the relationships Gottman was studying, they were romantic relationships. Imagine what it does when it's coming from a co-orker you spend 8 hours a day with, or a friend you've known for years, or a family member you can't just walk away from. That's what we're dealing with today. So, if contempt is this damaging, why don't we catch it sooner? [music] Why do most people spend months, sometimes years, around someone who makes them feel this way without ever being able to put their finger on what's actually happening? It's not because you're naive. It's not because you're weak. [music] It's because your brain is actively working against you in this situation. Here's what I mean. Your brain has a built-in bias toward resolving discomfort as quickly as possible. When something feels off, but you can't explain it, [music] your brain doesn't sit with that uncertainty. It fills in the gap. And almost always, it fills it in with the most comfortable explanation available. [music] So, when someone corrects you in front of a group, your brain says, "They were just being honest." When they look past you during a conversation, your brain says, "They were distracted. They're busy." It happens. When they respond to your good news with [music] nothing, your brain says, "Maybe they're going through something." You're not being gullible, you're being human. This is called politeness bias, and it's one of the most welldocumented patterns in social psychology. We are wired to interpret ambiguous behavior charitably, especially from people we're close to or people we respect. And contempt is almost always ambiguous. That's the whole point. Nothing is said directly. Nothing can be pointed to. Everything has a reasonable explanation if you're willing to look for one. Let me give you a concrete example. Imagine you're at dinner with a friend. You mention a new idea you've been excited about, something you've been working on for weeks, and they nod, take a sip of their drink, and say, [music] "Yeah, I've seen people try that before, and then they change the subject. What do you do with that?" There's nothing to object to. They didn't say you'd fail. They didn't say it was a bad idea. But you leave that dinner feeling deflated and your brain because it can't point to anything specific starts whispering. Maybe the idea really isn't that good. Maybe I'm just not seeing it clearly. That's the [music] loop. And once it starts, it's very hard to step out of. But here's what makes it worse. The more you care about someone, the harder it is to see clearly. There's something [music] called cognitive dissonance, which basically means that your brain struggles to hold two conflicting ideas at the same time. The idea that this person matters to you and the idea that this person thinks you're beneath them. Those two things can't both be true in your mind at the same time. [music] So, one of them has to give. And almost always, it's not the one that protects you. [music] So, instead of updating your view of them, you update your view of yourself. Maybe I am too sensitive. Maybe I did say something wrong. Maybe they're right and [music] I just can't see it. That loop, that self-doubt loop is exactly what contempt relies on. It doesn't need to be obvious. It just needs to be consistent enough to keep you questioning yourself instead of questioning them. And the really frustrating part, the more emotionally intelligent you are, the more you're at risk for this. Because empathetic people are better at finding explanations for other people's behavior. You're better at giving the benefit of the doubt. You're better at seeing things from their perspective. Those are genuinely good qualities, but in this specific dynamic, they work against you. Which is why being able to name what's happening, which is exactly what we're about to do, is so important. Because once you can name it, the loop breaks. You stop filling in the blanks for them, and you start seeing the pattern for what it actually is. So, let's get into the signs, the seven signs. All right, let's talk about the actual signs. I'm going to walk you through seven of them. Some will feel obvious once I say them out loud. Others are going to make you stop and go, "Oh, oh, that's what that was." Sign number one, they correct you in front of other people casually. You're in a group. You're telling a story or sharing an opinion or explaining something you know pretty well and they jump in. Not with anything dramatic, just a quiet, "Well, actually, [music] or I mean, it's a little more complicated than that." or even just m not exactly and suddenly the focus has shifted. Everyone's looking at them now [music] and you're standing there feeling like a student who got an answer wrong in class. Here's how you know this is contempt and not just someone being informative. Pay attention to when it happens. Do they correct you when it's just the two of you or does it almost always happen when there's an audience? Because what's actually going on in those moments isn't about accuracy. It's about positioning. [music] They're using you as a step to stand on. The correction isn't for your benefit. It's to establish [music] publicly that they know more than you do. And notice what they correct you on. Is it ever something that actually matters? Or is it always the small details, the exact date, the precise wording, the technicality that changes nothing about the point you were making? That precision isn't about truth. It's about reminding everyone in the room, including [music] you, who the authority is. Sign number two, they don't really look at you when you talk. This one is easy to miss because it feels too small to matter. [music] But think about a conversation with someone who genuinely likes you, someone who's happy to see you. They face you. Their eyes are on you. Their body is turned toward you. Now, compare that to the person we're talking about. When you're speaking, their eyes drift. [music] They check their phone. They glance around the room. They look at you for a second and then just past [music] you. And what this communicates below the level of words is whatever you're saying is not worth my full attention. [music] Now, here's what makes this especially insidious. If you call it out, it sounds petty. You weren't looking [music] at me. That sounds needy. That sounds like you're being oversensitive. Which is exactly why it works as a contempt signal. It's deniable. It's dismissible. [music] It gives them nothing to apologize for, but your nervous system registered it and it was right. [music] Sign number three, they ask for your opinion and then ignore it completely. This one stings in a particular way [music] because it involves a setup. They ask, you think they actually want to know. You share something real and [music] then nothing. They nod. Maybe they say h or yeah. In a way, that means they were never actually listening. And then they do whatever they were going to do anyway. The first time you give it a pass. Maybe they just had their mind made up already. The second time you start to wonder. By the third or fourth time, you start to shrink your answers. You stop putting in the effort. Because somewhere, without even realizing it, you've learned that your opinion in this dynamic isn't being collected, it's being performed. The question is theater. It creates the appearance of including you without ever actually including you. And here's what makes it especially hard. They can always say they asked. [music] I asked you what you thought. I always ask. And technically, they did. That's the cover, but asking and listening are two completely different things. [music] And you know which one you've been getting. Sign number four, the joke that isn't really a joke. Every group has this. The comment that gets a laugh or at least a smile and then lands just a little wrong in your chest. Oh, that's so you said in a tone that makes it clear you isn't a compliment. Don't worry, she always does this said to someone else about you while you're standing right there. [music] I'm kidding. Obviously, said after something that very clearly wasn't entirely a joke. [music] This is one of the most effective contempt tools available because it's wrapped in social protection. If you [music] react, you're the one who can't take a joke. If you call it out, you look oversensitive. If you laugh along, you've just endorsed it. So, what do you do with it? You stand there and absorb it. [music] And you tell yourself it was nothing. And you walk away feeling like something, but you can't name what. The tell, by the way, isn't the content of the joke. It's the target. Genuine humor punches in all directions. Contemptuous humor has a consistent target. And if you look back across your interactions with this person, you'll notice the target is almost always you. Sign number five, your good news gets a flat response. Okay, this one is quieter than the others, but it might be the most telling. [music] You share something you're excited about. Something you worked for, a promotion, a project you finished, [music] something that went well, and they say, "Oh, nice or cool. Good for you, and then nothing. No follow-up questions, no how did that happen?" [music] Or you must be so relieved. Just a flat acknowledgement and a pivot to something else. [music] Now, and this is the key part. Pay attention to how they respond when someone else shares good news. Is there suddenly more energy, more questions, more genuine warmth? Because people cannot fake enthusiasm equally. They will always give more to the people they actually care about. The enthusiasm gap, that difference in how they light up for others versus how they respond to you, that tells you exactly where you rank. This isn't about needing people to make a big deal out of everything you do. It's about the basic human instinct to respond to someone you care about with warmth when they're happy. When that warmth is just absent, specifically for you, that's data. [music] Sign number six. They help you in a way that makes you look smaller. This is the most subtle one on the list and honestly the one that took me the longest to understand [music] because how can someone helping you be a bad thing? Here's how. Genuine help is quiet. It builds you up and then gets out of the way. [music] The goal of real support is to make you more capable and more confident. Contemptuous help does the opposite. [music] It announces itself. It needs an audience. And it frames you even while helping you as someone who needs to be helped. [music] You know the move. Someone jumps in and says, "Here, let me explain this to her." Or, "Don't worry, he's still figuring this out." Or, "She's new to this." So, in a tone that's technically polite but unmistakably condescending. They're not wrong, maybe, but the way they deliver it [music] tells you everything. A person who respected you would find a way to help that didn't require announcing your limitations to everyone in the room. Watch for this, especially in professional settings. [music] When your colleague answers a question that was directed at you or when someone explains your own idea back to the room as if you hadn't just said it, that's not helpfulness. That's a quiet little power move dressed up as support. And over time, if you're around this dynamic enough, it does something insidious. It makes you doubt your own competence. Not because you're actually less capable, but because you keep being positioned as less capable. Other people start seeing you that way. And eventually, you start seeing yourself that way, too. Sign number seven, the micro expression you almost missed. Okay, this last one goes a little deeper. Stick with me. There's a psychologist named Paul Ecman who spent decades studying something called microexpressions. [music] These are tiny involuntary facial movements that flash across someone's face in a fraction of a second. We're talking faster than a blink. And they reveal what a person is actually feeling, [music] regardless of what expression they're trying to show you. Contempt has a very specific micro expression. It's the only one that's asymmetrical. One corner of the mouth pulls back very slightly. just one side, not a smile, not a smirk, really, just a flicker. And here's the thing. Ecman found that this expression is universal. It shows up in every culture across every background. You've seen it. Maybe you didn't know what it was. Maybe it happened in the middle of a normal conversation and you registered something but couldn't name it. That uneasy feeling you walked away with. That sense that something was off even though you couldn't point to anything specific. Your brain caught that microexpression and it filed it correctly. [music] The reason I want to end on this one isn't to make you paranoid. It's actually the opposite. I want you to trust yourself. [music] That instinct you've been second-guessing. That feeling that something was wrong when you couldn't find the evidence, it wasn't paranoia. It was pattern recognition and it was right. So now you're probably wondering why. Why would someone do all of this? Because understanding the why is actually what lets you stop taking it personally. Here's the uncomfortable truth. Contempt [music] almost always comes from insecurity. Not the kind of insecurity that looks like insecurity from the outside. The person doing this often looks extremely confident. They're composed. They're capable. [music] They probably have a lot of people around them who look up to them. But somewhere underneath that, there's a calculation happening. And the calculation goes, if I can position myself above you [music] consistently, quietly, in small ways that you can barely articulate, then I don't have to worry about being threatened by you. Your success makes them uneasy. Your presence in a room makes something in them compete. And instead of dealing with that internally, they manage it by keeping you just slightly diminished. Now, here's an important distinction. Some people do this deliberately. They know exactly what they're doing. They've developed contempt as a tool, a way of managing their social environment, and they deploy it consciously. But many don't. Some people have spent so long operating this way that these behaviors have become completely automatic. They correct people in public without thinking about it. They give flat responses to good news without realizing the message it sends. They've been doing this since long before they met you, and they'll keep doing it long after. [music] Does that make it okay? No. Does it make it less damaging? No. But it does mean something important. It was never actually about you. It wasn't triggered by something you did. It wasn't a verdict on your worth. It was a habit they brought into the room [music] and you happen to be there. It's about a gap in them that they're trying to fill at your expense. And now you see it for what it is. So what do you actually do with this? I'm not going to tell you to confront everyone who's ever made you feel small. That's not always realistic and honestly, it's not always necessary. What I will tell you is this. [music] The most powerful thing you can do is stop filling in the blanks for them. People who use contempt rely on your willingness to explain away their behavior. Your willingness to say, "Maybe I'm reading too much into it. [music] Maybe they didn't mean it like that. Maybe I'm being too sensitive." That generosity you keep extending to them, they've never once extended it to you. So, step one is simply this. Stop explaining it away. Not to punish them, to protect yourself. Call it what it is, at least internally. You don't have to say anything out loud. You don't have to make it dramatic. Just stop letting your brain file it under probably nothing. File it under what it actually is. Step two, notice how you feel after every interaction with them. Not during, after. Do you feel energized or do you feel drained? Do you feel more like yourself or slightly less? Your nervous system keeps score even when your brain is busy making excuses. This is worth being honest about because a lot of us are so used to certain relationships that we've stopped asking whether they're actually good for us. We measure relationships by how long they've lasted or by their official status in our lives. They're my friend, so it must be fine. But length and status aren't the [music] same as health. The question isn't how long you've known them. The question is, how do you feel after you leave? [music] And step three, and this is the one that actually matters most, redirect your energy toward the people who don't do this, [music] because here's what I found to be true. Once you really internalize what contempt looks like, you start noticing something else, too. You start noticing the people who are doing the opposite. [music] The ones who ask for your opinion and actually listen. The ones who light up when you share good news. The ones who help you without making you feel like you needed help. Those people have been there this whole time. But we spend so much energy trying to decode the people who make us feel small that we sometimes forget to invest in the ones who don't. [music] And here's what's interesting. When you shift your attention and energy toward those people, something else happens. Your own confidence starts to come back. [music] Not because they're complimenting you or building you up artificially, but because you're finally in an environment where you're not constantly having to recover from something, [music] where you're not spending mental energy monitoring interactions for signs of dismissal. That's not a small thing. That's actually what normal is supposed to feel like. If something in this video hit close to home, if you recognized a situation or a person while you were watching this, I want you to sit with that for a minute. [music] Not to feel bad, not to feel angry, but to feel clear, because that's what this is about. Not drama, not victim mentality, [music] just clarity. You were never imagining it. You were never too sensitive. you were reading the room correctly in a language that nobody ever taught you to name. Now you have the words. [music] If this was useful to you, let me know in the comments. And specifically, I'd be curious which one of the seven signs hit closest to home for you. I read every comment, and those conversations actually shape what I cover next. Take care of yourself, and I'll see you in the next one.
